title: A rare case of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in a patient with severe leptospirosis complicated with rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury; a case report
case_prompt:
A 21-year-old previously healthy male university student presented with 4 days of high fever with chills, rigors, and severe myalgia, and 1 day of oliguria with dark red urine. He had worked in a paddy field 10 days before admission. On examination, BMI was 22 kg/m2, temperature 101 °F, pulse 108 bpm, respiratory rate elevated, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. He was not pale or icteric and had no signs of fluid overload. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were normal; abdominal examination revealed severe generalized wall tenderness. Neurologic examination was unremarkable (GCS 15/15, normal fundi, no meningism). 

Laboratory studies showed severe metabolic acidosis on venous blood gas, serum creatinine 528 μmol/L, blood urea 15 mmol/L, WBC 11.3×10^9/L (89% neutrophils), platelets 84×10^9/L, CRP 126 mg/dL, creatine phosphokinase 390 000 U/L, and urine positive for myoglobin. He underwent hemodialysis on admission, with post-dialysis creatinine 260 μmol/L and urea 11 mmol/L, and was started on IV ceftriaxone. Over the next 4 days, fever and myalgia resolved but he remained anuric and dialysis-dependent; creatinine and urea stabilized around 200 μmol/L and 10 mmol/L, respectively, with decreasing CPK. Leptospira PCR was positive.

On hospital day 4, he developed a generalized headache and, a few hours later, sudden painless bilateral vision loss followed by several brief generalized tonic–clonic seizures. Between seizures he was confused and agitated. Neurologic exam now showed GCS 14/15 and complete bilateral blindness, with no meningism or papilledema. Blood pressure was 150/90 mmHg; other systems were normal. 

An urgent noncontrast CT scan of the brain showed no abnormalities, and venous blood gas revealed no major acid–base or electrolyte disturbances. Leptospirosis–related encephalitis, uremic encephalopathy, acid–base or electrolyte disturbance, and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome were considered.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Leptospirosis-related encephalitis was considered given the confirmed infection and new neurologic symptoms but was excluded once neuroimaging demonstrated vasogenic edema in a posterior distribution rather than inflammatory changes—“Leptospirosis with encephalitis, uremic encephalopathy, acid–base or electrolyte disturbance and PRES were major differential diagnoses at this point…The features were consistent with PRES.”
2. Uremic encephalopathy was considered in the context of acute kidney injury but was ruled out because “no major acid base or electrolyte disturbances were noted in the VBG.”
3. Acid–base or electrolyte disturbance was considered as a precipitant of seizures and vision loss but was excluded since “no major acid base or electrolyte disturbances were noted in the VBG.”
4. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome was confirmed by characteristic MRI findings of posterior subcortical white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities—“MRI of brain…showed T2/FLAIR high signal intensities in the left occipito-parietal and right temporo-parietal regions, involving mainly the subcortical white matter…and the features were consistent with PRES.”
